draft/06-summary.md:1:An inline liquid metering valve delivers a repeatable measured volume of concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and rinses the surfaces that contacted the concentrate after each dose, without any command additional to the stroke that delivers the dose.
draft/06-summary.md:3:The valve has a housing with an inlet and an outlet and a metering sleeve fixed within the housing. The metering sleeve defines a dose chamber, a concentrate port opening into the dose chamber, a carrier-liquid admission port opening into the dose chamber, and a flush bypass that opens downstream of the dose chamber. A piston slides axially in the dose chamber between a fill position and a discharge position. The piston has an upstream sealing land and a downstream sealing land axially spaced from one another and joined by a reduced-diameter waist.
draft/06-summary.md:7:The rinse is carried out by the return of the same piston. An annular rinse channel lies between an outer surface of the metering sleeve and an inner surface of the housing, and at least one rinse opening leads from that channel through the metering sleeve into the dose chamber. A follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet connected to the flush bypass during the return stroke, so that carrier liquid sweeps the annular rinse channel, issues from the rinse opening across the surfaces wetted by the concentrate, and leaves through the flush bypass to the outlet. The flush poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port to the dose chamber, so the rinse is complete, and the rinse liquid is on its way to the outlet, before any further concentrate can enter. The rinse cannot be omitted, mistimed or deferred, because the element that opens it is carried by the piston rod itself.
draft/06-summary.md:9:In described embodiments, a flexible lip on the upstream sealing land wipes the wall of the dose chamber before the flush poppet opens. Two radial rinse openings are directed across the concentrate port and across the one-way outlet valve.
draft/06-summary.md:13:A replaceable cartridge contains the piston, the metering sleeve, the one-way outlet valve and the flush poppet, and is retained by a threaded end cap. Removing the threaded end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the connections at the inlet and the outlet.
draft/06-summary.md:15:A corresponding method admits concentrate to the dose chamber, closes the concentrate port before uncovering the carrier-liquid admission port, expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve, and then opens the flush poppet with the follower pin during the return of the piston and closes it again before the concentrate port is reconnected.
draft/10-abstract.md:1:An inline liquid metering valve has a housing with an inlet and an outlet and a metering sleeve defining a dose chamber, a concentrate port, a carrier-liquid admission port and a flush bypass opening downstream of the dose chamber. A piston sliding in the dose chamber has two sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist. In a fill position the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while the lands isolate the carrier-liquid admission port. Movement toward a discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so carrier liquid passes behind the measured volume and expels it through a one-way outlet valve. On the return stroke a follower pin on the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet, rinsing the wetted surfaces through an annular rinse channel and closing before the concentrate port is reconnected.
draft/04-field.md:1:The present disclosure relates to inline liquid metering valves, and more particularly to a reusable valve that delivers a repeatable measured volume of a concentrate into a flowing carrier liquid and that rinses the internal surfaces wetted by the concentrate as part of the same mechanical cycle.

Claim 1 is unchanged this turn and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. content.text:
All four findings are fixed, entirely within the figure briefs; no application text changed.

**Radial discharge into the rinse channel (critical).** In FIG. 2 the one-way outlet-valve passage now leads from the dose chamber into the upper band and is broken off at a break line within the band, so what it opens into is not indicated. FIG. 3 does the same for its outlet-valve passage, and the flush bypass now runs from the poppet into the upper band toward the outlet end and is likewise broken off within the band. Neither passage is drawn crossing the sleeve wall into the inlet-fed annular rinse channel, so the depicted topology no longer contradicts the flow paths recited in the detailed description and claims 1 and 13. This is the same neutral convention FIG. 2 already used for the carrier-liquid admission port.

**FIG. 1 end-cap location (major).** The disclaimer now covers the axial matter as well as the radial one: the axial end at which the end cap ring and the mouth receiving the removable unit are drawn is a convention only, and no relationship between the end cap and either line connection is intended.

**Negative flow boundary (minor).** The clause stating that the bypass passage has no other opening to the bore is deleted.

**FIG. 4 groove convention (minor).** The helical cam groove band is now drawn in broken line throughout, consistent with the wholly hidden follower pin that engages it and with the brief's own statement that the groove surface is not indicated. The follower-pin bullet is unchanged.

Each of the four briefs grew with these fixes, so I offset the additions by removing depiction constraints that had no source behind them and identified no part: a hatching-stop instruction and two page-position modifiers on lead lines in FIG. 1, a duplicated "in the position shown" and a redundant contact phrasing in FIG. 3, and several instances of "conventional" before "break line". All four briefs are now within the length limit at 2783, 2653, 2788 and 2756 characters. Numeral sets, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions, the detailed description and the claims are unchanged and still match one another.

input.summary: All four findings are fixed and every one of them was confined to the figure briefs; the application text, the numeral table and the claims are untouched. The critical flow-topology defect is gone: in FIG. 2 the one-way outlet-valve passage now leads from the dose chamber into the upper band and is broken off at a break line within the band so that what it opens into is not indicated, and FIG. 3 does the same for both its outlet-valve passage and the flush bypass, which now runs from the flush poppet into the upper band toward the outlet end and is broken off within the band. Neither passage is drawn crossing the sleeve wall into the inlet-fed annular rinse channel any longer, so the depicted topology matches the flow paths recited in the detailed description and in claims 1 and 13. The FIG. 1 disclaimer now reaches the axial matter as well as the radial one, stating that the axial end at which the end cap ring and the mouth receiving the removable unit are drawn is a convention only and that no relationship between the end cap and either line connection is intended. The untraced negative clause that the bypass passage has no other opening to the bore is deleted. In FIG. 4 the helical cam groove band is now in broken line throughout, which is consistent with the wholly hidden follower pin that engages it and with the brief's own statement that the groove surface is not indicated. Because each fix lengthened its brief, I offset the additions by removing depiction constraints that had no source behind them and identified no part: a hatching-stop instruction and two page-position modifiers on lead lines in FIG. 1, a duplicated position phrase and a redundant contact phrasing in FIG. 3, and several instances of conventional before break line. All four briefs are within the length limit at 2783, 2653, 2788 and 2756 characters, the per-sheet numeral sets are unchanged, and no note, placeholder or em dash appears anywhere in draft/ or figures/. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the application carries no citations and, as the drafting brief records, the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: The critical finding was about where two passages were drawn discharging, and the honest fix was to stop the drawing from answering a question the inventor never answered. The disclosure says the flush bypass opens downstream of the dose chamber and that rinse liquid leaves through it to the outlet; it never says which way the passage runs out of the sleeve, and it never places the one-way outlet valve. Breaking each passage off inside the wall band leaves the disclosed function visible and the undisclosed destination unstated, which is the same convention FIG. 2 already used for the carrier-liquid admission port.

I fixed this in the drawing rather than by adding a routing sentence to the specification. Writing a path for either passage into the description would have imported structure the inventor never gave, and the claims already recite the flow from the rinse channel through the rinse opening and the flush bypass to the outlet, which is all the support the figures need to conform to.

On FIG. 1, the existing disclaimer disclaimed only radial position, so it did not reach the choice that put the end cap, the cartridge withdrawal mouth and the inlet at the same axial end. That choice decides which line connection the cartridge passes on removal, which is technical substance, and the inventor says only that removing the end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the housing connections. Extending the disclaimer to the axial end keeps the drawing usable without asserting the relationship.

The negative clause about the bypass having no other opening to the bore came in earlier to force a renderer to gate the poppet properly. It was doing a job, but it stated a contact topology the source never characterises, and the positive description that the poppet stands between the bore and the passage now carries that job on its own.

On FIG. 4 the two bullets were describing mutually exclusive constructions: a groove outlined as an outer-surface feature and a pin hidden along its whole length. Making the groove band broken line throughout resolves it in the direction that asserts nothing, which is what the brief's own disclaimer of the groove surface requires. The pin bullet stayed as it was.

Every trim I made to fit the length limit came out of rendering control rather than physical geometry: where a lead line sits on the page, whether hatching stops at a panel outline, and repeated phrases. The bodies, contacts, openings, break lines and occlusions the sheets must show are all still stated positively.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still rests on the axial order in which the concentrate port closes before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, and on the follower pin carried by the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke with the poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. The Background states the technical problems the invention addresses without attributing any of them to a publication. Claim 1 is unchanged this turn and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. reasoning: The critical finding was about where two passages were drawn discharging, and the honest fix was to stop the drawing from answering a question the inventor never answered. The disclosure says the flush bypass opens downstream of the dose chamber and that rinse liquid leaves through it to the outlet; it never says which way the passage runs out of the sleeve, and it never places the one-way outlet valve. Breaking each passage off inside the wall band leaves the disclosed function visible and the undisclosed destination unstated, which is the same convention FIG. 2 already used for the carrier-liquid admission port.

I fixed this in the drawing rather than by adding a routing sentence to the specification. Writing a path for either passage into the description would have imported structure the inventor never gave, and the claims already recite the flow from the rinse channel through the rinse opening and the flush bypass to the outlet, which is all the support the figures need to conform to.

On FIG. 1, the existing disclaimer disclaimed only radial position, so it did not reach the choice that put the end cap, the cartridge withdrawal mouth and the inlet at the same axial end. That choice decides which line connection the cartridge passes on removal, which is technical substance, and the inventor says only that removing the end cap withdraws the cartridge without disturbing the housing connections. Extending the disclaimer to the axial end keeps the drawing usable without asserting the relationship.

The negative clause about the bypass having no other opening to the bore came in earlier to force a renderer to gate the poppet properly. It was doing a job, but it stated a contact topology the source never characterises, and the positive description that the poppet stands between the bore and the passage now carries that job on its own.

On FIG. 4 the two bullets were describing mutually exclusive constructions: a groove outlined as an outer-surface feature and a pin hidden along its whole length. Making the groove band broken line throughout resolves it in the direction that asserts nothing, which is what the brief's own disclaimer of the groove surface requires. The pin bullet stayed as it was.

Every trim I made to fit the length limit came out of rendering control rather than physical geometry: where a lead line sits on the page, whether hatching stops at a panel outline, and repeated phrases. The bodies, contacts, openings, break lines and occlusions the sheets must show are all still stated positively.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still rests on the axial order in which the concentrate port closes before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, and on the follower pin carried by the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke with the poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port.

content.text:
Both findings are fixed.

**FIG. 4 detent recesses (major).** The brief no longer says which collar surface carries the recesses or from which direction the detent element enters them. The recesses are now shown schematically as plain recesses at three angular positions at one station along the collar's length, with the surface on which they are formed, their depth and profile, and the entry direction expressly not indicated. The detent bullet now reads as a plain detent element engaging that recess, with no contact relationship beyond the engagement itself indicated. This matches how the same brief already treats the cam groove and the stop faces. Target 48 was reworded to "engaging" to stay in step. The application text needed no change: claim 8 recites the detent and the three recesses as separate elements, and the description says only that the detent engages one of the three recesses to retain the selected setting.

**Claim 7 (minor).** Claim 7 now recites "each of the three selectable axial stop faces, when selected, limiting travel of the piston to set a respective dose volume", so it no longer reads as all three limiting travel at once. That agrees with the description, with claim 9's "a selected one of the three selectable axial stop faces", and with claim 18. No other claim changed.

Adding the two disclaimers pushed FIG. 4 over the brief length limit, so I recovered the space from constraints that identify no part: two instances of "conventional" before "break line", the curved-edge rationale, the direction in which the outer numeral patches curve, a verbose restatement of the stop-face order disclaimer, and four over-specified lead-line targets, which are now broad interior targets on the intended parts. FIG. 4 is 2764 characters; the other three briefs are unchanged at 2783, 2653 and 2788. Numeral sets, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions and the detailed description remain synchronized.

That matches the treatment the same brief already gives the cam groove and the stop faces. Target 48 was reworded from seated in to engaging so the leader description stays in step. Claim 7 now recites that each of the three selectable axial stop faces, when selected, limits travel of the piston to set a respective dose volume, so it no longer reads as all three limiting travel simultaneously, and it agrees with the description, with claim 9 and with claim 18. Adding the two disclaimers pushed FIG. 4 past the 2800-character brief limit, so I recovered the space from constraints that identify no part: two instances of conventional before break line, the rationale attached to the collar's curved end edge, the direction in which the outer numeral patches curve, a verbose restatement of the stop-face order disclaimer, and four over-specified lead-line targets, which are now broad interior targets on the intended parts. FIG. 4 is 2764 characters and the other three briefs are unchanged at 2783, 2653 and 2788. reasoning: The FIG. 4 finding was about the brief being inconsistent with itself. It disclaimed the collar surface carrying the cam groove and the end carrying the stop faces, then turned around and put the detent recesses on the curved outer surface with the detent entering them radially from outside. The inventor gives the detent and the recesses as a function only, so the fix was to extend the same neutralization already used twice in that brief rather than to invent a construction.

I kept the three angular positions at one axial station, because that much is forced: a single fixed detent has to meet a different recess at each of three rotational increments. What I removed was only the surface and the entry direction, which nothing in the disclosure decides.

Claim 7 was a drafting slip rather than a support problem. Reading each of three stop faces as limiting travel at the same time is physically impossible, and the description, claim 9 and claim 18 all already said one selected face governs at a time. Adding when selected fixes the reading without narrowing anything, since the claim always meant the collar carries three faces of which the presented one sets the dose.

I made no change to the description for either finding. The description was already neutral about where the recesses sit and already said the stop face presented by the current increment of rotation limits travel, so editing it would have been churn on text that was correct.

The length trims all came out of rendering control rather than physical geometry. The four target rewrites also serve the endpoint guidance directly: pointing numeral 40 at the collar body clear of the groove and recesses, and numeral 42 at the interior of the groove band, are broad interior targets, where the previous wording added an away-from-the-pin modifier and a visible-surface modifier that no source decides.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still rests on the axial order in which the concentrate port closes before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, and on the follower pin carried by the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke with the poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. The Background states the technical problems the invention addresses without attributing any of them to a publication. Claim 1 is unchanged this turn and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. The specification explains the problem each solves before it is needed. The dependent ladder retreats first to the two directed rinse openings and the flexible-lip wipe, then to the waist-out-of-register interval and the express axial-ordering recitation, then to the self-indexing collar with cam groove, stop faces, detent and window, and finally to the cartridge and threaded end cap. The claim 7 amendment clarified that the selected face governs at any given time and did not narrow the collar-and-stop-face fallback. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run for this matter, so the art available here may be incomplete and the claims should be re-checked against any later search results.

View: enlarged longitudinal section of the metering portion of FIG. 1 during the return stroke, axis horizontal, with the flush poppet held open. The index collar is omitted for clarity. All line work lies well inside the drawing area.

Geometry:

- The housing wall appears in section as upper and lower hatched housing bands, the sleeve wall inside as upper and lower hatched sleeve bands spaced inward; between them is the bore.
- The clear gap between the sleeve and housing bands is the annular rinse channel, supplied with carrier liquid from the inlet end.
- In the left half of the bore, the piston is drawn as two hatched enlarged portions joined by a narrower middle portion, with a plain shaft extending leftward past the sleeve's left end and a short pin on it.
- Thin flexible projections extend from the left portion to the bore walls: the flexible lip, shown without flare direction.
- An opening through the upper sleeve band, its inner mouth clear of the sealing lands so that the rinse opening beneath it discharges across that mouth, is the concentrate port, with a short stub rising from it, broken off. The waist is not in register with the opening.
- A passage leads from the bore into the upper sleeve band and is broken off at a break line within that band, so that what it opens into is not indicated, with a plain closure element across it: the one-way outlet valve, unnumbered.
- Adjacent the left end of the sleeve, a plain closure element shown schematically is the flush poppet, held open by the pin and standing between the bore and a plain passage that runs from it into the upper sleeve band toward the outlet end and is broken off at a break line within that band, so that what it opens into is not indicated: the flush bypass.
- Two openings through the lower sleeve band connect the rinse channel to the bore: one adjacent the concentrate port and one adjacent the outlet-valve passage, each clear of the sealing lands.
- A further opening through the lower sleeve band, covered by the right portion of the piston, its outer mouth broken off within that band: the carrier-liquid admission port, unnumbered.
- Which sleeve band each port and passage is drawn in is a section-plane convention only; no circumferential relationship between them is intended.

content.text:
The finding is fixed.

**Band naming in the section views (FIG. 3, with FIG. 2 for consistency).** FIG. 3 now names the two pairs of bands distinctly: the housing wall appears as upper and lower hatched housing bands, and the sleeve wall inside as upper and lower hatched sleeve bands. Every port and passage that the description locates in the metering sleeve wall now names that wall explicitly: the concentrate port and the one-way outlet-valve passage in the upper sleeve band, the flush-bypass passage running into the upper sleeve band, and the two rinse openings and the carrier-liquid admission port in the lower sleeve band. The break-off phrases read "within that band", tied to the sleeve band named in the same sentence. The rinse-channel bullet now reads as the clear gap between the sleeve and housing bands, target 60 as the clear gap between the lower housing and sleeve bands, and the section-plane sentence as which sleeve band each port and passage is drawn in. A renderer following the brief can no longer put any of those features through the housing wall.

FIG. 2 received the same treatment for the one bare reference the review noted plus the two others in the same file: the outlet-valve passage and its break line now name the upper sleeve band, the admission port's break line reads "within that band", the sleeve is introduced as upper and lower hatched sleeve bands, the housing as hatched housing bands, and target 22 names the upper sleeve band. FIG. 1 now calls the sleeve's bands sleeve bands and targets 18 on the hatched upper sleeve band, so the naming is uniform across all four sheets.

The added words pushed FIG. 3 over the brief length limit, so I recovered the space from wording that identifies no part: the view line's note that the index collar is omitted (the sheet carries no collar numerals), a redundant "in the position shown" and a "conventional" before "break line", and a shortened phrase for the piston portion covering the admission port. All four briefs are within the limit at 2783, 2662, 2796 and 2764 characters. No application text changed, as the review indicated none was required, and the numeral table, per-sheet numeral sets, drawing descriptions and detailed description remain synchronized.

input.summary: Fixed the reported band-naming defect and carried the same naming through the other section views so no bare band reference remains anywhere. In figures/FIG-3.md the housing wall is now introduced as upper and lower hatched housing bands and the sleeve wall as upper and lower hatched sleeve bands, and every feature the description locates in the metering sleeve wall names that wall: the concentrate port and the one-way outlet-valve passage in the upper sleeve band, the flush-bypass passage running into the upper sleeve band, and the two rinse openings and the carrier-liquid admission port in the lower sleeve band, with each break-off phrase reading within that band. The rinse-channel bullet reads as the clear gap between the sleeve and housing bands, target 60 as the clear gap between the lower housing and sleeve bands, and the section-plane sentence as which sleeve band each port and passage is drawn in. figures/FIG-2.md received the same treatment for the outlet-valve passage the review named and for the two other bare references in that file, and its sleeve and housing bands are now named, with target 22 naming the upper sleeve band. figures/FIG-1.md now calls the sleeve's bands sleeve bands and targets 18 on the hatched upper sleeve band. A renderer following any brief can no longer put the ports, the outlet-valve passage or the flush bypass through the housing wall. The added words pushed FIG. 3 past the 2800-character brief limit, so I recovered the space from wording that identifies no part: the view line's note that the index collar is omitted, on a sheet that carries no collar numerals, a redundant in the position shown, a conventional before break line, and a shortened phrase for the piston portion covering the admission port. All four briefs are within the limit at 2783, 2662, 2796 and 2764 characters. No application text changed, since the review indicated none was required, and the numeral table, the per-sheet numeral sets, the drawing descriptions and the detailed description remain synchronized. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so the application carries no citations and, as the drafting brief records, the art available to this draft may be incomplete.
reasoning: The defect was that FIG. 3 spent its opening bullet assigning the phrase upper and lower hatched bands to the housing and then used the bare phrase for sleeve-wall features. A renderer obeying the brief's own antecedent would have pierced the housing wall with the concentrate port, the outlet-valve passage, the flush bypass and the admission port, which the description and claim 1 put in the metering sleeve. Naming both pairs of bands and qualifying every later reference removes the ambiguity without asserting anything new.

I extended the fix to the two other bare references in FIG. 2 and to the band wording in FIG. 1 even though the review named only one. Leaving a single unqualified band reference in a neighbouring sheet would reintroduce the same failure mode, and the change is purely nominal, so there was no reason to fix the class of error halfway.

I made no change to the description, the claims or the numeral table. The text already says the concentrate port is a radial port through the wall of the metering sleeve 18, that the sleeve defines the flush bypass 26, and that the rinse openings 62 pass through the sleeve wall. The drawing specification was the outlier, so the drawing specification is what changed.

The length trims came out of rendering control rather than geometry. The collar-omission note was the cheapest cut because FIG. 3 carries no collar numerals, so nothing in the numeral accounting depends on it, and the state the figure depicts is already fixed by the view line's during the return stroke, with the flush poppet held open.

Claim 1 is unchanged and still rests on the axial order in which the concentrate port closes before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, and on the follower pin carried by the piston rod opening the normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke with the poppet closing before the waist reconnects the concentrate port.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. The Background states the technical problems the invention addresses without attributing any of them to a publication. Claim 1 is unchanged this turn and continues to rest on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. The specification explains the problem each solves before it is needed. The dependent ladder retreats first to the two directed rinse openings and the flexible-lip wipe, then to the waist-out-of-register interval and the express axial-ordering recitation, then to the self-indexing collar with cam groove, stop faces, detent and window, and finally to the cartridge and threaded end cap. This turn's edits were confined to naming in the figure briefs and touched no claim and no scope. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run for this matter, so the art available here may be incomplete and the claims should be re-checked against any later search results.

content.content:
1	Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.
2	
3	Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.
4	
5	The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.
6	
7	Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.

Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices are often set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. A screw setting can be lost during cleaning and gives no indication of what was set. An electronic setting requires power, a sensor and a display at the valve, which is unwelcome in wet, washdown or hazardous locations, and it tells the operator only what the controller believes rather than what the mechanism will actually deliver.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Devices that rely on separately actuated shut-off elements to keep the two sides apart depend on those elements being commanded in the correct order, so a control fault, a lost signal, or a slow-acting element can open both sides at once.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Where the two sides are kept apart by separately actuated shut-off elements, the separation depends on those elements being commanded in the correct order.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. The usual remedy is to break the valve out of the line and clean it by hand, which takes the installation out of service and exposes the person doing the work to the concentrate. Where a rinse is provided at all, it is commonly a separate operation that has to be commanded after the dose, and it therefore depends on an operator or a controller performing an extra step at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

+The cartridge 64 contains the piston 28, the metering sleeve 18, the one-way outlet valve 38 and the flush poppet 58, and is removable from the housing 12 as a unit. Removing the threaded end cap 66 withdraws the cartridge 64 from the housing 12 without disturbing the connections at the inlet 14 and the outlet 16, so that the cartridge 64 is replaced as a unit while the housing 12 remains in the line.

In use, carrier liquid flows through the housing 12 from the inlet 14 to the outlet 16. With the piston 28 in the fill position, concentrate is admitted through the concentrate port 22 and past the waist 34 into the dose chamber 20 to form a measured volume, the upstream sealing land 30 and the downstream sealing land 32 isolating the carrier-liquid admission port 24 from the concentrate port 22. The piston 28 is then advanced toward the discharge position so as to close the concentrate port 22 and thereafter to uncover the carrier-liquid admission port 24 with the downstream sealing land 32. Carrier liquid is admitted through the carrier-liquid admission port 24 behind the measured volume and expels the measured volume through the one-way outlet valve 38 toward the outlet 16. The extent of the travel available to the piston 28, and therefore the measured volume, is fixed by the selected one of the three axial stop faces 46.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Where the two sides are kept apart by separately actuated shut-off elements, the separation depends on those elements being commanded in the correct order.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. That film drips into the carrier stream between doses, so the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured. It also dries, crystallizes, or reacts on the wetted surfaces, so that a valve which was accurate when new drifts, sticks, or seizes in service. Where the valve must be broken out of the line and cleaned by hand, the installation is taken out of service; and where a rinse is a separate operation commanded after the dose, it depends on that operation being performed at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

file.content:
Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Where the two sides are kept apart by separately actuated shut-off elements, the separation depends on those elements being commanded in the correct order.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, may retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. Where such a film passes into the carrier stream between doses, the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured; and where it dries or reacts on the wetted surfaces, the accuracy of the valve changes in service. Where the valve must be broken out of the line and cleaned by hand, the installation is taken out of service; and where a rinse is a separate operation commanded after the dose, it depends on that operation being performed at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

Many liquid handling installations add a small, accurately measured quantity of a concentrate to a much larger stream of a carrier liquid that is already flowing in a pipe. The concentrate may be aggressive, staining, strongly colored, biologically active, or simply expensive, and the quantity that must be added is small in comparison with the carrier flow. The addition therefore has to be made repeatably, without measuring the concentrate by eye, and without allowing the concentrate to reach any part of the installation other than the carrier stream itself.

Two practical difficulties dominate this kind of dosing. The first is separation of the two liquids upstream of the point of addition. A dosing device sits between a concentrate source and a pressurized carrier line, and any path that momentarily connects the two allows carrier liquid to be forced back into the concentrate source or allows concentrate to migrate into the carrier line at a time when no dose is called for. Where the two sides are kept apart by separately actuated shut-off elements, the separation depends on those elements being commanded in the correct order.

The second difficulty is residue. The surfaces that the concentrate touches, in particular the port through which it enters the metering volume and the seat of the check element through which the dose leaves, may retain a film of concentrate after the dose has been delivered. Where such a film passes into the carrier stream between doses, the quantity actually added is not the quantity that was measured; and where it dries or reacts on the wetted surfaces, the accuracy of the valve changes in service. Where the valve must be broken out of the line and cleaned by hand, the installation is taken out of service; and where a rinse is a separate operation commanded after the dose, it depends on that operation being performed at the right moment.

Dose selection presents a further difficulty. Adjustable dosing devices may be set by a screw or by an electronically stored value. There remains a need for a setting that is retained by the mechanism itself and that is visible at the valve without electronics.

There remains a need for an inline metering valve in which the separation of the concentrate from the carrier liquid is enforced by the geometry of the moving parts rather than by the order in which external commands arrive, in which the surfaces wetted by the concentrate are rinsed by the carrier liquid as an unavoidable part of the return of the metering element, and in which the selected dose is both retained and displayed mechanically.

content.text:
I ran the full text-side filing gate against the current application and found no defect to fix, so I changed nothing.

**What I verified**

- *Figure and sheet numbering.* Exactly four figures are described, FIG. 1 through FIG. 4, in draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md, and figures/ holds exactly FIG-1.md through FIG-4.md. No gap, no extra figure, no reference to a figure that has no brief.
- *Reference numerals.* draft/numerals.md defines 29 numerals, 10 through 66, one part each and one name per part. Every one is used in the detailed description. The per-figure sets recited in the description match each brief's numeral list exactly: FIG. 1 has 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 52, 64, 66; FIG. 2 has 18, 20, 22, 24, 30, 32, 34, 38; FIG. 3 has 22, 26, 28, 44, 56, 58, 60, 62; FIG. 4 has 36, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54. No sheet carries more than eight. Where a numeral appears on two sheets it labels the same part on both: 18 the sleeve band, 22 the concentrate-port opening, 44 the follower pin.
- *Leader endpoints.* Every numeral listed on a sheet has exactly one target in that sheet's Targets list, and each target names the part that numeral labels in the table and the description. The targets are broad interior points on the intended parts.
- *Text-to-drawing relationships.* The view line of each brief matches its caption in draft/07-drawings.md. Every port and passage in the section views names the sleeve band or housing band it passes through, matching the description's placement of the ports and the flush bypass in the metering sleeve. Neither FIG. 2 nor FIG. 3 is taken on a designated section line, both being enlargements of the FIG. 1 metering portion, so no cutting-plane line, designation or arrows are called for.
- *Filing formalities.* Twenty claims, apparatus 1 to 12 and method 13 to 20, with sound antecedent basis and no means-plus-function language; every claim term appears in the description; the abstract is a single paragraph of 145 words; cross-reference and government support both read "Not applicable."; no note, placeholder, question or em dash anywhere in draft/ or figures/; no citations, since prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references. All four briefs are within the length limit at 2783, 2662, 2796 and 2764 characters.

**What I could not do**

The one open blocker is that no drawing sheet has been rendered and review/figure-audit-evidence.json does not exist. Figure files in this workspace are Markdown specifications; the sheets are produced from them by the image pipeline, and I do not create image files. So I cannot regenerate the sheets, cannot run the pixel-level checks that depend on them (OCR of the numerals, leader endpoint landing, hatching, drawn geometry), and cannot clear the two mechanical failures, which report the 29 numerals as absent from every drawing only because no drawing file exists to read them from. The briefs are complete and ready to render exactly as written; I did not add, move or redistribute any numeral, since the existing mapping is already one-to-one and within the per-sheet limit, and redistributing it would break a correct plan.

The package is therefore not publishable this turn. It needs a render pass over the four briefs, followed by the pixel audit against those images.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is no document to cite and none is cited anywhere in the application. The Background is conditional or need-framed throughout: it states the separation hazard, the residue problem and the dose-setting problem as technical situations the invention addresses, without asserting facts about third-party devices that nothing in the workspace supports. Claim 1 rests on two concrete relationships expressed in the inventor's own terms rather than in generic dosing-valve vocabulary. The first is that the axial order of the sealing land faces and the port edges closes the concentrate port before the downstream sealing land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so that no position of the piston places the concentrate source in communication with the carrier-liquid path and the separation does not depend on the order in which external commands arrive. The second is that a follower pin carried by the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet during the return stroke and the poppet closes before the waist reconnects the concentrate port, so the rinse of the concentrate-wetted surfaces is compelled by the same stroke that delivers the dose rather than being a separately commanded operation. The dependent ladder retreats first to the two directed rinse openings and the flexible-lip wipe, then to the waist-out-of-register interval and the express axial-ordering recitation, then to the self-indexing collar with cam groove, stop faces, detent and window, and finally to the cartridge and threaded end cap. Nothing in the claims changed this turn. The drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run for this matter, so the art available here may be incomplete and the claims should be re-checked against any later search results.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

1	An inline liquid metering valve has a housing with an inlet and an outlet and a metering sleeve defining a dose chamber, a concentrate port, a carrier-liquid admission port and a flush bypass opening downstream of the dose chamber. A piston sliding in the dose chamber has two sealing lands joined by a reduced-diameter waist. In a fill position the waist connects the concentrate port to the dose chamber while the lands isolate the carrier-liquid admission port. Movement toward a discharge position closes the concentrate port before the downstream land uncovers the carrier-liquid admission port, so carrier liquid passes behind the measured volume and expels it through a one-way outlet valve. On the return stroke a follower pin on the piston rod opens a normally closed flush poppet, rinsing the wetted surfaces through an annular rinse channel and closing before the concentrate port is reconnected.
